subject: Archaeology
title: Ramesses the Great: Builder King
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Ramesses the Great: Builder King.

hook.text: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years and built more monuments than any pharaoh in history.

buildup.text: He carved his name on temples across Egypt — and sometimes carved over other pharaohs' names too.

discovery.text: He signed history's first known peace treaty after the Battle of Kadesh against the Hittites in 1274 BCE.

twist.text: His mummy shows he had arthritis, dental abscesses, and was over 90 when he died — ancient by any standard.

climax.text: In 1974, his mummy was flown to Paris for restoration. Egypt issued him a passport listing his occupation as 'King.'

punchline.text: A 3,000-year-old king got a passport and flew to Paris.

quiz.question: What historical first is Ramesses II credited with?
options: Building the first pyramid in Egyptian history
Signing history's first known peace treaty
Being the first pharaoh to be mummified

details.summary: Ramesses II ruled Egypt for sixty-six years, building more monuments than any other pharaoh including Abu Simbel and expansions at Karnak and Luxor. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh and signed history's first known peace treaty.
details.whyItMatters: Ramesses II's long reign and massive building program make him the most visible pharaoh in the archaeological record. His monuments define the popular image of ancient Egypt worldwide.
takeaways: Ruled for sixty-six years, the longest major pharaonic reign
Built Abu Simbel and expanded Karnak and Luxor temples
Signed the first known international peace treaty

faq.question: What happened at the Battle of Kadesh?
faq.answer: Ramesses II fought the Hittite Empire around 1274 BCE in modern Syria. Though Ramesses claimed total victory, the battle was likely a draw. The resulting peace treaty, preserved in both Egyptian and Hittite versions, is the oldest surviving international agreement.

faq.question: Why did Ramesses build so many monuments?
faq.answer: Monumental building demonstrated divine favor and pharaonic power. Ramesses also re-carved earlier pharaohs' statues with his own name, inflating his visible legacy. His sixty-six-year reign gave him more time to build than any predecessor.
